q: Which policies of the East India Company were chiefly responsible for the political causes of the Revolt of 1857?
o: Permanent Settlement and Ryotwari Settlement
Ilbert Bill and Vernacular Press Act
Doctrine of Lapse, Subsidiary Alliance and Effective Control
Charter Act of 1833 and Charter Act of 1853

q: The Religious Disabilities Act of 1856, which caused socio-religious resentment before the Revolt of 1857, provided that:
o: Widow remarriage would be legalised
Christian missionaries would require government licences to preach
A change of religion would not debar a son from inheriting his father's property
Sati would be made a criminal offence

q: Which of the following 'outside events', in which the British suffered reverses, is believed to have psychologically emboldened Indians before the Revolt of 1857?
o: The First Afghan War (1838-42), Punjab Wars (1845-49) and the Crimean War (1854-56)
The Anglo-Mysore Wars
The Battle of Plassey and Battle of Buxar
The Anglo-Maratha Wars

q: The immediate spark for the Revolt of 1857 was:
o: The passage of the General Service Enlistment Act, 1856
The annexation of Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse
The introduction of greased cartridges for the Enfield rifle, rumoured to contain cow and pig fat
The imposition of income tax on Indians

q: Nana Saheb, who led the revolt at Kanpur, was:
o: A native of Madras who settled in Faizabad
The adopted son of the last peshwa, Baji Rao II
The zamindar of Jagdishpur
The deposed nawab of Awadh

q: At Lucknow, the rebellion (which broke out on June 4, 1857) was led on behalf of whom by Begum Hazrat Mahal?
o: General Bakht Khan
Maulvi Ahmadullah
Her son Birjis Qadir, who was proclaimed nawab
Her husband, the deposed nawab of Awadh

q: Rani Laxmibai of Jhansi took up arms against the British primarily because:
o: Her husband Raja Gangadhar Rao was imprisoned by the British
She was denied the title of peshwa
The British imposed the Enfield rifle on her troops
Lord Dalhousie refused to recognise her adopted son's succession and annexed Jhansi under the Doctrine of Lapse

q: Khan Bahadur, who led the revolt at Bareilly with an army of about 40,000 soldiers, was:
o: The adopted son of Baji Rao II
A native of Madras settled in Awadh
The zamindar of Jagdishpur
A descendant of the former ruler of Rohilkhand

q: Shah Mal, a local leader in Pargana Baraut (Baghpat, Uttar Pradesh) during the Revolt of 1857, is notable for:
o: Organising headmen and peasants of 84 villages (chaurasi desh) against British hegemony
Proclaiming himself peshwa at Kanpur
Leading the siege of the Lucknow Residency
Commanding the sepoy court at Delhi

q: Which of the following is correctly identified as a reason for the failure of the Revolt of 1857?
o: Absence of any civilian involvement
Absence of an all-India character, with the east, south and west remaining largely unaffected
Complete lack of participation by sepoys
Overwhelming superiority of Indian arms and equipment

q: Which of the following Indian rulers did NOT join the Revolt of 1857 and, in some cases, actively helped the British?
o: Kunwar Singh and Khan Bahadur
Begum Hazrat Mahal and Maulvi Ahmadullah
Nana Saheb and Rani Laxmibai
The Sindhia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore and the Maharaja of Kashmir

q: According to one estimate cited in the chapter regarding the geographic and demographic reach of the Revolt of 1857:
o: The revolt affected all provinces of British India equally
More than three-fourths of India's area was directly affected
Only Delhi and its immediate vicinity were affected
Not more than one-fourth of the total area and one-tenth of the total population was affected

q: Which of the following factors is cited as contributing to the poor military performance of the rebels during the Revolt of 1857?
o: The British had no experienced commanders
The rebels had no sepoy participation at all
The rebels possessed superior artillery
Rebels were poorly equipped, generally fighting with swords and spears against British Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph

q: During the Revolt of 1857, Hindu-Muslim unity was notably demonstrated by:
o: The exclusive participation of Muslim sepoys in the revolt
Separate and rival administrations set up by Hindus and Muslims
The complete absence of Muslims from leadership positions
The universal acknowledgement of Bahadur Shah Zafar, a Muslim, as emperor by both Hindu and Muslim rebels, and the banning of cow slaughter in rebel-controlled areas

q: According to Marxist historians, the Revolt of 1857 has been characterised as:
o: A war exclusively between rival feudal lords
A struggle of the soldier-peasant democratic combine against foreign imperialism as well as indigenous landlordism
A movement led entirely by the educated middle class
A purely bourgeois-nationalist movement

q: Which of the following is a direct consequence of the Revolt of 1857 with respect to constitutional changes?
o: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's trading rights
The Pitt's India Act, 1784 established dual control
The Act for the Better Government of India, 1858, transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown
The Regulating Act of 1773 was passed

q: Following the Revolt of 1857, British military policy was reorganised around the concept of:
o: Abolition of separate caste/community-based units
Universal conscription of Indians into a single unified force
'Division and counterpoise', increasing European troops and recruiting from so-called 'martial races'
Complete disbandment of the British Indian Army

q: The 'White Mutiny' after the Revolt of 1857 refers to:
o: A protest by British civilians against the Queen's Proclamation
An uprising of European planters against indigo cultivation reforms
Unrest among European Company troops who resented the compulsory transfer of allegiance to the Crown and the stoppage of batta allowances
A revolt of Indian sepoys who refused to accept British commissions

q: The Indian Civil Service Act of 1861, passed in accordance with the Queen's Proclamation, is best described as:
o: Nominally promising equality of opportunity but in practice keeping higher services largely reserved for the colonisers
Opening half of all civil service posts to Indians immediately
Establishing reserved constituencies for Indians in the civil service
Abolishing the civil service examination system entirely

q: Which of the following best summarises the overall significance of the Revolt of 1857 for the course of Indian nationalism?
o: It directly led to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1857 itself
It ended all British interest in ruling India
It had no lasting impact on Indian political consciousness
It was not a coordinated national war of independence, but it established local traditions of resistance and helped forge an early sense of collective political identity
